label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's National Pharmacare Program: What the Pharmacare Act Has Actually Delivered

review.sentence: It is a short framework statute, and the most important thing to understand about what it has "delivered" is what it does not do: it appropriates no money of its own, sets no dollar figure, and creates no entitlement to a drug.
review.why: Section 6(3) of the Act expressly provides that amounts payable under the payment obligation "may be paid by the Minister out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund", and the bill's Recommendation speaks of "the appropriation of public revenue" for the measure — so the statute does carry its own (open-ended) spending authority. No note supports "appropriates no money of its own".

review.sentence: Everything that has actually reached a pharmacy counter in Canada flows from a separate bilateral agreement between the federal government and a province or territory, signed after the Act passed.
review.why: The Act's preamble records that the federal government already provides drug coverage "within federal jurisdiction ... to certain populations", and s.5 commits funding to Indigenous peoples as well as provinces and territories — so coverage reaching patients does not all flow from post-2024 bilateral agreements. None of the notes supports the universal claim.

review.sentence: The second phase — the broader formulary that a single-payer system would require — is not defined in the Act and, on the evidence gathered here, has no funding attached to it.
review.why: The Act does set up the second phase: s.8 requires the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential drugs to inform a national formulary within one year, and s.11 requires a committee of experts on the operation and financing of national universal single-payer pharmacare, which reported in 2025 (the Final Report of the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts). The section leaves both out.

review.sentence: (Inference, not a claim in the statute: this is why the rollout has been uneven across the country, since each province bargains separately and can decline.)
review.why: The section attributes uneven rollout solely to provinces declining, but by spring 2026 the federal Spring Economic Update showed no new funding for additional pharmacare deals (bilateral health funding falling from $4.3bn in 2025-26 to $3.1bn in 2027-28) and Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said "the door was closed on our province" — the federal side has also stopped signing.

review.sentence: BC's is the largest by a wide margin and the only one in which the province added something of its own beyond the federal terms — free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms.
review.why: The Manitoba release — the source the section itself cites for Manitoba — says "As part of this agreement, Manitoba will also provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to residents." So BC is not the only jurisdiction that added something beyond the federal contraception/diabetes terms.

review.sentence: Coverage was to begin no later than January 2026 — the latest start date of the four.
review.why: The Yukon release (the cited source) does not say this, and the BC release says BC residents would begin receiving coverage in March 2026 — later than Yukon's January 2026. Yukon's start date is second-latest, not the latest.

review.sentence: Ontario and Alberta are the significant omissions by population and by politics: Alberta's government has publicly opposed a national pharmacare program in principle, and Quebec's approach has been to insist on full compensation with no conditions.
review.why: No note supports any of this: the CCPA piece names New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Ontario as forgoing money and gives no account of Alberta's or Quebec's positions. The sentence also pairs Ontario with Alberta as "the two", then discusses Alberta and Quebec.

review.sentence: Second, the CCPA's later analysis reported no new signatories and noted that overall federal bilateral health funding falls from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28, so the pharmacare ramp-up is happening inside a shrinking bilateral health envelope [4].
review.why: The same CCPA analysis says there will be "no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals," that existing agreements appear set to expire without renewal (PEI's minister cited $29 million in cuts; Newfoundland and Labrador was told "the door was closed"), which contradicts the section's "ramp-up" framing and is central to who is left outside and whether the four deals survive.

review.sentence: The short answer is that nobody has published a number of people enrolled or using the program, and the federal government's own pharmaceutical page does not try.
review.why: The section's own source publishes a utilization count: BC reports approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024 and more than 306,000 since the program began. A published number of people using the coverage therefore does exist; the claim needs narrowing to the federal government's own reporting.

review.sentence: British Columbia: no reach figure given for the agreement itself, but the province reported about 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024 under its own pre-existing program — the closest thing to a real utilization number in any of the material [9].
review.why: The cited BC release does give reach figures for the agreement itself: it "will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians" and "nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes." Saying no figure was given is contradicted by [9].

review.sentence: Summed, those four announcements describe roughly 580,000 people in the eligible pool (my arithmetic: 350,000 + 227,000 + 41,000 + 12,000 for contraception, and 149,000 + 16,000 + 3,000 for diabetes), in a country of about 41 million.
review.why: The sum uses 227,000 (BC's actual 2024 utilization) in place of BC's announced reach of more than 1.3 million for contraception and nearly 550,000 for diabetes, so the total understates the announced eligible pool by roughly 1.7 million people. The arithmetic also adds a utilization count to three projected figures.

review.sentence: Anyone reading the first-year number as the steady-state cost of the program will understate it by a factor of three.
review.why: $269.6 million against $88.1 million is a factor of about three, but the section calls 2028-29 a projected figure and then treats it as the steady state; the CCPA source says the federal government appears poised to let the agreements expire without renewal, so 2028-29 is a peak, not a demonstrated steady state.

review.sentence: Spread over an eligible pool of roughly 580,000 people, that is about $150 per person per year (my arithmetic).
review.why: The per-person figure inherits the wrong denominator. Using the reach figures the agreements actually announced (about 2.3 million people once BC's 1.3 million and 550,000 are included), the same $88.1 million is closer to $40 per person, which undermines the comparison that follows with the cost of diabetes supplies.

review.sentence: So the honest state of the evidence is: four agreements, about $928 million committed over four years, about $88.1 million spent in the first year, roughly 580,000 people eligible, and no published count of anyone actually using it.
review.why: The section reads the transfers as ramping toward a steady state but omits the CCPA's central finding that there will be no new federal pharmacare funding, that bilateral health funding falls from $4.3B to $3.1B by 2027-28, and that the four agreements may expire without renewal — which changes what "committed over four years" means.

review.sentence: The gross incremental cost to public plans is $14.8 billion rising to $17.3 billion; the net figure after displaced private spending and the economy-wide savings is the $11.2–13.4 billion above [7].
review.why: PBO gets from $14.8–17.3B to $11.2–13.4B by accounting for savings on direct federal spending and Pharmacare copayment revenues, not by subtracting displaced private spending or the economy-wide savings — the $1.4–2.2B economy-wide savings are a separate comparison of total drug spending against the status quo baseline, not a deduction from public cost.

review.sentence: The second costs a full single-payer universal drug plan — every prescription, replacing existing public and private plans.
review.why: PBO's model covers the RAMQ formulary, not "every prescription" — and the same report shows the formulary choice drives the total: a full single-payer universal plan on a catastrophic formulary costs only $1.8B in 2024-25 rising to $2.0B in 2027-28, roughly a sixth of the RAMQ figure.

review.sentence: So there is no PBO number for "the federal share of full pharmacare" — anyone who quotes one has invented the split.
review.why: The note only says the 2023 report cannot isolate federal costs under an undetermined cost-sharing model; the PBO has in fact published "Federal Cost of a National Pharmacare Program" (2017), which the 2023 report describes as the estimate it updates, so a PBO federal-cost number does exist.

review.sentence: The CCPA has been the main non-governmental estimator, and its numbers are in the same range as the PBO's full-program work while differing in distributional detail.
review.why: The CCPA pages cited here contain no full-program cost estimate at all: they give $928M as the value of four signed agreements and per-province forgone-transfer estimates (Ontario ~$2.5B over four years). Nothing in them is "in the same range" as $11.2–13.4B a year.

review.sentence: The first is the honest comparison to what has been legislated; the second is what "national pharmacare" in the full sense would cost.
review.why: The section presents $11.2–13.4B as the price of full pharmacare without noting that the same PBO report costs full single-payer plans on two other formularies — catastrophic ($1.8B rising to $2.0B) and essential medicines — so the headline range reflects a RAMQ-formulary choice, not pharmacare in the abstract.

review.sentence: The CCPA's July 2025 analysis put signed agreements at $928 million over four years [3], against a PBO full-program cost of $11.2–13.4 billion a year [6] — a ratio that makes the point better than any argument: what has been signed so far is roughly 2% of one year of a real program, spread over four years.
review.why: This compares unlike quantities — a federal transfer envelope for four jurisdictions over four years against the PBO's combined federal-plus-provincial incremental public cost for one year — the very federal/provincial conflation the section warns against two paragraphs earlier.

review.sentence: Its consistent argument is that the federal envelope is far below what a universal plan costs and that non-signing provinces are forgoing money they would otherwise receive — with Ontario alone forgoing an amount in the billions over four years.
review.why: The best-known independent estimate of a comprehensive plan points the other way and is left out: the 2019 National Advisory Council report "A Prescription for Canada" estimated Canada would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs by 2027 with a comprehensive formulary while improving access — an independent estimate that belongs in this section.

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act (2024) actually established, and what it committed the federal government to fund

The Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) received Royal Assent on 10 October 2024 [3]. It is a short framework statute, and the most important thing to understand about what it has "delivered" is the shape of the obligation it creates: a conditional transfer authority, not a benefit and not a fixed appropriation.

Section 6(1) obliges the Minister to pay a province or territory only "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so", and ties the money to a defined purpose: to "increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1]. Section 6(3) then supplies the spending authority in open-ended terms: any amount payable under 6(1) "may be paid by the Minister out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund at the times and in the manner, and on any terms, that the Minister considers appropriate" [1]. The bill's Recommendation likewise speaks of "the appropriation of public revenue" [1]. So the Act does carry its own spending authority — but it is authority without a number, without a ceiling, and exercisable only once a province signs. That combination is why the program's real size is set by negotiation rather than by statute.

Section 5 is where a reader looking for a national commitment would expect it to be defined, and it is deliberately loose: the Government of Canada commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases, and funding for provinces and territories must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments [1]. There is no amount, no escalator and no schedule. A commitment to maintain funding is not a formula, and nothing in the section gives a province a claim on a future dollar.

The Act is also not silent on the second phase, and this is routinely missed. Section 8 requires the Minister, after discussions with the provinces and territories, to ask the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare "no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1]. Section 9 requires a national bulk purchasing strategy on the same one-year clock, section 10 a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy, and section 11 a committee of experts on "options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare", reporting within a year and tabled in Parliament [1]. So the statute does schedule the architecture of a full program. What it does not do is fund any of it: the formulary list, the purchasing strategy and the expert report are planning instruments, and the CCPA records that the 2025 Final Report of the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts has since joined the 2018 parliamentary committee report and the 2019 Advisory Council report in recommending a universal single-payer system — recommendations that were not followed by funding [4].

The preamble is worth reading for a related reason. It records that the Government of Canada already "provides, within federal jurisdiction, health care services, including coverage for prescription drugs and related products, to certain populations" [1] — First Nations and Inuit, veterans, military personnel, the RCMP, refugees and federal inmates. Those federal drug programs predate the Act and continue; section 5 also commits funding to Indigenous peoples directly. So federal pharmacare money reaching patients is not all post-2024 bilateral money, and the agreements are an addition to a pre-existing federal role rather than the creation of one.

One correction to a common framing: the Act is not a spending bill that was then implemented. It is a conditional-transfer authority plus a planning mandate. The federal dollars appear as transfers under the agreements (Section 2), and the coverage is delivered by provincial drug plans under provincial rules. The Act sets the terms of the bargain — contraception and diabetes, first-dollar, universal within the participating jurisdiction — and leaves the formulary details and timing to each negotiation.

It is also now clear that the constraint on the program's reach has not been provincial reluctance alone. By spring 2026 the federal side had stopped signing: the CCPA's Andrew Longhurst reports that from the Spring Economic Update there appears to be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals, with bilateral health funding dropping from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [4]. Both sides of the table matter to the explanation for uneven rollout, and the federal budget is now the binding one. (Inference, not a claim in any source read here: because the Act's payment obligation is triggered only by agreement, a federal decision not to conclude further agreements is sufficient on its own to keep nine jurisdictions outside, whatever those provinces want.)

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, on what terms, for how much, and who is still outside

Four jurisdictions have signed. In signing order: Manitoba (27 February 2025), British Columbia (6 March 2025), Prince Edward Island (7 March 2025) and Yukon (20 March 2025). All four deals were struck within a four-week window in early 2025, all under the Trudeau Liberal government [4]. As of a July 2025 accounting by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, "just four provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements with the federal government. Those agreements are valued at $928 million over four years starting in 2026" [3]. My own addition of the four announced amounts — $219 million (Manitoba), $670 million (BC), $30 million (PEI) and $9.5 million (Yukon) — comes to roughly $928 million, matching the CCPA total, so the four figures reconcile.

**Manitoba — more than $219 million over four years.** Announced 27 February 2025 as the first national pharmacare agreement: "the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [8]. The total Manitoba package was $267 million across two agreements, the second providing over $48 million for rare-disease drugs [8]. Manitoba residents were told to expect coverage for the majority of products in June 2025, and the release framed reach as nearly 350,000 Manitobans for contraception and over 149,000 people with diabetes [8]. Manitoba also added free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to residents as part of the agreement [8] — a detail worth flagging, because HRT is not a federal requirement and at least two jurisdictions added it.

**British Columbia — more than $670 million over four years.** Announced 6 March 2025: a deal "to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [9]. BC's is the largest by a wide margin — roughly 72% of the total signed envelope — and its reach figures are correspondingly large: more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [9]. BC also added free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms "for all residents" [9]. Coverage under the agreement was to begin in March 2026 [9]. BC had a head start: the province began providing free contraceptives on 1 April 2023, and approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024 alone, with more than 306,000 having benefited since the program began [9].

**Prince Edward Island — more than $30 million over four years.** Announced 7 March 2025 as part of a $40 million package that also included over $10 million for rare-disease drugs: the federal government would provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them, with funding also improving access to diabetes devices and supplies [10]. Coverage was expected from 1 May 2025 — the earliest start date of the four. PEI framed the reach as over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes [10]. Its health minister described the deal as building on the existing Provincial Diabetes Drug Program, a useful reminder that these agreements expand provincial plans rather than create a federal one [10].

**Yukon — up to $9.5 million over four years.** Announced 20 March 2025, to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for Yukon residents, with funding also improving access to diabetes devices and supplies [11]. Coverage was to begin no later than January 2026 [11]. Yukon framed the reach as more than 12,000 residents for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes [11]. Note the "up to": Yukon's is a ceiling, unlike the others' "more than."

The four start dates, in order, were PEI (May 2025), Manitoba (June 2025), Yukon (no later than January 2026) and BC (March 2026) [8][9][10][11]. BC's is the latest, not Yukon's, which matters for anyone trying to work out when a given province's residents actually began paying nothing.

**Who is outside, and why the list stopped growing.** Nine jurisdictions had no pharmacare agreement as of the July 2025 CCPA analysis: Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Northwest Territories and Nunavut [3]. Two different accounts of why the list stopped at four are in circulation, and they are not equally supported.

The first account, implied by the CCPA's July 2025 piece, is that provinces are refusing money, and that piece puts figures on what they forgo: "New Brunswick would likely receive $136 million through a bilateral pharmacare agreement over four years. Nova Scotia would receive $171 million, and Ontario would receive an estimated $2.5 billion over four years" [3]. Those are the CCPA's own per-capita estimates of the transfer each non-signing province would get, not published federal allocations. The second, which the CCPA itself published in May 2026, is that the federal government stopped offering it. Longhurst writes that from the Spring Economic Update it appears there will be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals, with bilateral health funding dropping from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [4]. He adds two specific confirmations from provincial health ministers: in April, PEI's health minister revealed that Ottawa will be cutting $29 million in health care funding to the province over the next three years, and after PEI raised the issue publicly, Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said the door was closed on that province [4]. Longhurst's conclusion is that the federal government appears poised to let the existing agreements expire without renewal, which would force the four participating jurisdictions to fund the coverage themselves or end it [4].

On the evidence read here, the second account is the better-supported explanation for the current state, and the first was the better-supported explanation for 2025. Both were true at different times: in the year after Royal Assent, four provinces signed and others did not; by 2026, the federal budget line was falling and the offers had stopped. Anyone attributing the nine-jurisdiction gap solely to provincial politics is working from 2025 evidence.

**What has actually been spent.** The announced totals are commitments, not outlays, and the agreements are back-loaded. "In 2025-26, the federal government contributed $88.1 million to support these provinces and one territory in the expansion of public coverage of diabetes medications and contraception for all residents. The federal pharmacare contribution is expected to increase to $269.6 million by 2028-29" [4]. Two things follow. First, in the first full fiscal year the federal government spent $88.1 million against $928 million committed — roughly 9.5% of the envelope (my arithmetic). Second, $269.6 million in 2028-29 is a projected peak, not a demonstrated steady state, and the same CCPA analysis says the agreements may not be renewed at all [4]. The trajectory is therefore better described as a four-year ramp that may terminate than as a program scaling to permanence.

### 3. What is actually covered: the contraception and diabetes formulary, devices, and how it sits on top of provincial plans and private insurance

The Act's coverage promise is narrow and specific, and the agreements implement it in almost identical language. What is covered is a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications, plus, in the agreements signed so far, diabetes devices and supplies [8][9][10][11]. Nothing beyond that. No cancer drugs, no antibiotics, no cardiovascular medication, no mental-health formulary — those remain where they were, in provincial plans, private insurance, or nowhere.

**Contraception.** The federal releases describe coverage as universal and first-dollar: no cost at the pharmacy counter for the covered products. The clearest statement of what that means in practice comes from PEI's Minister Responsible for the Status of Women, who said that through the agreement "more contraceptives, including long-acting reversible contraceptives such as IUDs and some hormonal options, will be more freely available" [10]. Two things are worth drawing out. First, the inclusion of long-acting reversible contraceptives matters more than the pill, because LARCs have high upfront costs (hundreds of dollars for a device plus insertion) and are the contraceptive method with the strongest evidence for reducing unintended pregnancy — a first-dollar plan removes the exact barrier that suppressed their use. Second, the phrase "some hormonal options" is a hedge: the formulary is a list, not "all contraception," and which hormonal products appear on it is a provincial formulary decision.

**Diabetes.** Coverage runs to medications plus devices and supplies — meaning test strips, lancets, insulin pens and, depending on the provincial list, insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors. This is a materially bigger commitment than pills alone, because diabetes supplies are recurring monthly costs and are the part of diabetes care most often rationed by people paying out of pocket. PEI's agreement explicitly ties the funding to devices and supplies as well as medications [10]; Yukon's does the same [11].

**What the agreements do not cover.** The Act's first phase excludes the drugs that dominate private drug spending — biologics, oncology, and the expensive rare-disease therapies that a separate $1.5 billion National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases handles. That separation is explicit in the PEI announcement, where the pharmacare agreement (over $30 million) sits alongside a rare-disease agreement (over $10 million) inside a $40 million package, with the rare-disease side naming specific drugs — Poteligeo, Epkinly and Koselugo — and noting that "Innovative treatments for rare diseases can cost anywhere from $100,000 to more than $4 million per year" [10]. Anyone reading the pharmacare headline number as though it buys modern specialty medicine is reading it wrong.

**How it sits on top of existing coverage.** This is the part most often misunderstood, and the statute is clear: the federal money is to "increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage" for the covered products [1]. It is additive, not substitutive. Three consequences:

First, no province's existing plan was replaced. PEI's health minister described the deal as building on the province's existing Provincial Diabetes Drug Program [10]; BC had already been providing free prescription contraception to roughly 227,000 people in 2024 before federal money arrived, and its agreement layered federal funding on top while the province added free hormone replacement therapy for menopause [9]. Manitoba did the same: as part of its agreement, Manitoba also provided free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to residents [8]. HRT is not a federal requirement in the Act, so two of the four jurisdictions have gone beyond the contraception-and-diabetes floor. Manitoba's release pointed to coverage beginning in June 2025 on top of its existing programs [8].

Second, private insurance was explicitly assumed to stay in place. The PBO's first-phase costing rests on the assumption "that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms" [5]. So the plan is not a single payer in the first phase, whatever the Act's language about "single-payer" coverage says: it is a federal first-dollar layer sitting under or alongside workplace plans, with the federal government picking up the residual cost for the uninsured and the cost-related non-adherent.

Third, "universal" in this context means universal within a participating province, not across Canada. Health Canada's own framing is that the Minister "will continue working with PTs to reach bilateral agreements to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar access" — a description of a negotiation in progress, not of a national entitlement [10]. A resident of Ontario and a resident of Manitoba are, as of the evidence here, in different systems for contraception and diabetes.

That produces an odd distributional result, flagged as inference: the federal government is paying 100% of the cost of contraception and diabetes drugs for residents of four jurisdictions that already had partial coverage, while paying nothing for residents of nine jurisdictions, including the three largest provinces. The money follows the signature, not the need.

### 4. How many people are actually enrolled and using it, and what the published numbers do and do not show

The honest answer has two halves. The federal government publishes no count of people enrolled or using the program. One province does publish utilization, and its numbers are the only measured evidence in the record.

Health Canada's prescription-drugs page, dated 5 November 2026, says only that "Canada has signed pharmacare agreements with a number of provinces and territories. The agreements will make a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications available for free or at low cost at pharmacies" [2]. There is no enrollment count, no registration figure, no claims volume, no utilization total, and no per-province breakdown of people reached. That absence is itself a finding: the federal published record describes what the agreements make *available*, not what has been *used*.

The structural reason is that a first-dollar layer on an existing provincial plan requires no registration. A resident walks into a pharmacy with a prescription and a health card and pays nothing. That is good policy design and poor measurement design: because there is no enrolment step, there is no administrative count of participants. The only organisations that can produce a utilization figure are the provincial drug plans and the pharmacies, through claims data. (Inference: the absence of a federal count follows from the program's no-registration structure.)

**The reach figures announced with each agreement** are estimates of eligible population, not counts of users:

- Manitoba: nearly 350,000 Manitobans for contraception and over 149,000 with diabetes [8].
- British Columbia: more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [9].
- Prince Edward Island: over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes [10].
- Yukon: more than 12,000 residents for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes [11].

Adding the four announcements gives an eligible pool in the range of 1.7 million people for contraception and roughly 0.7 million for diabetes (my own arithmetic on the figures in [8], [9], [10] and [11]). BC accounts for roughly three-quarters of both totals, which reflects both its population and how broadly it counted eligibility.

**The one published utilization count is BC's.** BC began providing free contraceptives on 1 April 2023, before any federal money. "In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [9]. Three things follow. First, this is a real utilization number, and it is the only one in the material read for this report — no other jurisdiction, and no federal department, has published an equivalent. Second, it predates the federal transfers, so it measures BC's own program, not the pharmacare agreement, whose coverage began in March 2026 [9]. Third, it is small relative to BC's announced eligible pool: 227,000 users against more than 1.3 million eligible in 2024, or about 17% (my arithmetic). That gap between eligibility and use is the single most informative number here, and it is worth being careful about what it means. It may reflect that most of the 1.3 million are men or otherwise not contraceptive users — the eligible pool is defined by sex and age, not by demand — so 17% is not a take-up rate and should not be read as one. What can be said is that no source read here establishes take-up, and BC's figures are the only place one could begin to estimate it.

**What the transfers actually buy.** The 2025-26 federal contribution across all four jurisdictions was $88.1 million [4]. Spread over the roughly 1.7 million people the agreements describe as eligible for contraception coverage, that is about $52 per person for the year; spread over the combined eligible pool of about 2.4 million people across both categories, about $37 (my arithmetic, and crude, since the money is not allocated per head). Either way the first-year per-person figure is low, and the reason is the ramp: $269.6 million is projected for 2028-29 [4]. Anyone reading the first-year number as the steady-state cost will understate it by a factor of about three — while anyone treating 2028-29 as the steady state will overstate it, since the CCPA reports the agreements may expire without renewal [4].

**Why utilization matters more than announcement numbers.** The program's stated purpose is not to make a list available but to remove cost as a barrier to adherence. The PBO's first-phase model is built explicitly on the group who do not fill prescriptions for cost reasons, assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions [5]. If the program is working, the measurable outcome is a fall in cost-related non-adherence for contraception and diabetes drugs in the four participating jurisdictions — and that has not been published by anyone. Health Canada repeats the same baseline in every release: in 2021, Statistics Canada found that one in five adults in Canada did not have the insurance they needed to cover their medication costs [10]. The CCPA's 2026 analysis adds context on the size of the problem: Canadian residents spent $8 billion on out-of-pocket prescription drugs in 2023, another $15.8 billion went through private plans, and estimates from 16 studies put cost-related non-adherence at five to 10 per cent of the population, two to five times higher than in comparable countries with universal pharmacare [4]. None of that is a post-program measurement.

So the state of the evidence is: four agreements, about $928 million committed over four years, $88.1 million spent in 2025-26, an eligible pool of roughly 1.7 million for contraception and 0.7 million for diabetes, one provincial utilization count (BC: 227,000 people in 2024, 306,000 since 2023), and no federal count of anyone using the program. The gap between "available" and "used" remains the central unmeasured quantity in Canadian pharmacare — and because the federal side has stopped signing, it may never be measured for the four jurisdictions as a group.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost, and why the estimates differ

Two different PBO estimates get conflated in public argument, and they answer different questions. The first costs the first phase — contraception and diabetes only, layered on existing coverage. The second costs a full single-payer universal drug plan on the Quebec RAMQ formulary, replacing existing public and private plans. The first is the honest comparison to what has been legislated; the second is what a full program on a broad formulary would cost. A third set of PBO numbers shows that even the second is a formulary choice rather than a fixed price.

**The first-phase estimate: $1.9 billion over five years.** The PBO's costing note on Bill C-64, published in May 2024, found that the first phase of national universal pharmacare would increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years, and stated its central assumption: "This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms" [5]. That assumption is the whole ballgame. Because the model assumes nobody loses existing coverage, the federal government only pays for the gaps: "The new program will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons. The latter group is assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions" [5]. For people already covered, the program pays only the out-of-pocket portion. The underlying data is IQVIA 2021-22 spending on diabetes and contraception drugs, projected forward using PMPRB price-growth factors [5]. The note flags high uncertainty and excludes behavioural substitution — people using more contraception or more diabetes medication once the price falls to zero — and excludes any new federal rebates.

So the $1.9 billion is a *gap-filling* estimate, not a program cost. It is the cost of making an existing patchwork free at the margin, not the cost of building a plan. Anyone citing it as the price of pharmacare is misreading it.

**The full-program estimate on a RAMQ formulary: $11.2 billion rising to $13.4 billion a year in incremental public cost.** The PBO's 2023 report modelled a genuine national plan under the framework the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health set out in 2016: universal, replacing existing public and private drug plans, using the RAMQ formulary as the national formulary, with a $5 copayment for brand-name prescriptions and exemptions for children, students, seniors, pregnant women, people with disabilities, EI recipients and social assistance recipients [7]. Under that model, "the additional cost to the public sector is estimated to be $11.2 billion in 2024-2025, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-2028" [6]. Total drug expenditure under pharmacare is estimated at "$33.2 billion in 2024-25 (the assumed first full fiscal year of implementation), increasing to $38.9 billion in 2027-28" [7]. The gross cost incremental to public drug plans is $14.8 billion rising to $17.3 billion; "after accounting for savings on direct federal spending and Pharmacare copayment revenues," the net incremental public cost falls to the $11.2–13.4 billion range [7]. That is the correct bridge between the two figures, and it is worth stating precisely because it is often mis-stated: the offset is direct federal savings (the Public Service Health Care Plan, federal population coverage, the medical expense tax credit) plus copayment revenue — not displaced private spending, and not the economy-wide savings.

Two features of the report matter for reading every other number in this debate. First, it refuses to split the bill: "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs" [7]. The report also notes that the incremental cost could be borne entirely by the federal government or split, depending on the cost-sharing model adopted [7]. Second, the public-payer cost is not the economy-wide cost. The PBO's headline finding was that economy-wide savings can be achieved under a single-payer universal drug plan even as the public payer's incremental cost rises, with savings of $1.4 billion in 2024-25 rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28 [6]. Total drug spending in 2024-25 is estimated at $33.2 billion under pharmacare versus $34.6 billion under the baseline [7]. The mechanism is that a single payer negotiates prices down to the lowest in Canada, applies confidential rebates to the private and out-of-pocket share, and enforces generic and biosimilar substitution — and because private-plan drug expenditures historically grow faster than public ones (5.8% versus 5.3%), the savings widen over time [7]. That distinction — public cost up, total cost down — is the most important thing in the PBO work and the thing most often dropped from both sides of the political argument.

One correction to a claim sometimes made: a PBO federal-cost number for pharmacare does exist historically. The 2023 report describes itself as an update of the PBO's 2017 "Federal Cost of a National Pharmacare Program," prepared on the same HESA framework [7]. The 2023 report's refusal to isolate federal cost is a statement about the 2023 model's undetermined cost-sharing, not a claim that no federal estimate has ever been published.

**The number depends on the formulary, by a factor of six.** The 2023 report also costs two alternative formularies, and the results are not close. On a catastrophic formulary — drugs that could cause undue financial hardship, drawn from the lists used by BC, Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador and PEI — "the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [7]. On an essential medicines formulary, dominated by generics whose prices are already low, drug expenditures come out $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion *more* than baseline in 2024-25 and 2027-28, because the increase in utilization is not offset by savings from negotiating power [7]. So the range across the three PBO formularies runs from about $1.8 billion to about $11.2 billion in the same year. The $11.2–13.4 billion headline is the price of a broad, RAMQ-style formulary; it is not "the cost of pharmacare" in the abstract, and citing it without the formulary is citing a modelling choice as a fact.

**Why the first-phase and full-program estimates differ.** The gap between $1.9 billion over five years and $11–13 billion per year is not a disagreement about arithmetic; it is a difference in what is being costed. The first-phase number covers two drug classes and preserves private insurance. The full-program number covers a broad formulary and abolishes private insurance for covered drugs. The first-phase figure works out to under $400 million a year on average (my arithmetic on $1.9 billion over five years); the full-program figure is roughly thirty times that. Comparing them as if one refutes the other compares a down payment to a purchase price.

**The government's own envelope, and the independent estimates.** The 2024 budget set aside $1.5 billion over five years for pharmacare — less than the PBO's $1.9 billion first-phase estimate. (Inference: the announced funding did not cover the announced coverage. The PBO note does not itself make this comparison in the passages read here.) The actual transfers confirm the scale: $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to peak at $269.6 million by 2028-29 [4].

On independent estimates, two need separating. The CCPA has not published a full-program cost estimate in the material read here; what it publishes is the value of the signed agreements ($928 million over four years) [3], the actual and projected transfers [4], and an argument about forgone funding — its July 2025 piece is about provinces refusing hundreds of millions, with per-province figures for what non-signing jurisdictions forgo [3]. Its consistent argument is that the federal envelope is far below what a universal plan costs, but the number it puts on the program is the signed envelope, not a model of the whole system. So the CCPA is not an independent full-program estimate in the way the PBO is, and it should not be cited as one.

The best-known independent estimate that points the other way is the 2019 National Advisory Council report, *A Prescription for Canada*, which the CCPA itself cites: it "estimated that by 2027, with a comprehensive formulary of drugs, Canada would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs while at the same time improving access for all" [4]. That is a national-total saving, not a public-payer cost, and it is broadly consistent with the PBO's finding of economy-wide savings — though the PBO's saving is smaller ($2.2 billion by 2027-28), because the PBO models a $5 copayment and a RAMQ rather than comprehensive formulary. Anyone quoting the $5 billion figure should quote the PBO's $2.2 billion alongside it, since the two are the same kind of number measured under different assumptions.

**What the numbers mean together.** The first phase, fully implemented across all thirteen jurisdictions, would cost the federal government something under $2 billion over five years. The full program on a broad formulary would cost the public sector $11–13 billion a year, offset by $1.4–2.2 billion of economy-wide savings, and on a catastrophic formulary about a sixth of that. What has been signed is $928 million over four years for four jurisdictions [3] — roughly 2% of one year of the broad-formulary program. That comparison has to be made carefully, because it sets a four-year federal transfer envelope for four jurisdictions against a one-year combined federal-and-provincial cost for the whole country; it is an order-of-magnitude illustration, not a ratio. But the order of magnitude is the point, and it is not in dispute between the PBO and the CCPA.
