report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone restrictions, and what the rules actually require

The first thing the record shows is that the policy question has largely been settled politically while the evidence question is still open. By 2026, "roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access" [2]. An earlier count, cited in the SMART Schools study, put it at "one in four countries (including France, Israel, and Turkey, as well as regions of Canada and Australia)" with laws mandating that public schools prohibit phone use during the school day [3]. The gap between one-in-four and more-than-half is not a contradiction: it is roughly two years of rapid adoption, and it means almost any evaluation of these policies is measuring something implemented recently enough that long-run effects cannot yet exist.

The jurisdictions also are not doing the same thing, and the differences are large enough to explain why evaluations disagree. Three distinct instruments are visible in the primary documents, and they differ in legal force, in the part of the day they cover, and in what they do about storage.

#### Ontario: a policy memorandum under the code of conduct

Ontario's rule is Policy/Program Memorandum 128, issued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024 [6]. It is a memorandum under the provincial code of conduct, not a statute — it binds school boards by directing the local policies they must adopt, rather than creating an offence.

Its substantive rule differs by grade, which is unusual among the jurisdictions surveyed here. For grades 7 to 12, "the local policy must require that for grades 7 to 12 students’ personal mobile devices are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time" [6]. The restriction is confined to instructional time, so phones are permitted at breaks and lunch in secondary school. For younger grades the memorandum extends the requirement across the school day.

The definition of the device is deliberately wide: "personal mobile device refers to any personal electronic device that can be used to communicate or to access the Internet, such as a cellphone, tablet, laptop or smartwatch" [6]. A smartwatch is covered, and so is a school-issued laptop used for something other than the lesson.

There are three exceptions, and they are the ones that recur across every jurisdiction: use "for educational purposes, as directed by an educator", "for health and medical purposes", and "to support special education needs" [6]. The special-education carve-out is the one that matters most in practice, because a phone is a support tool for a meaningful number of students — timers, reminders, communication apps, blood-glucose monitoring — and a rule written without it would fail those students first.

Ontario's memorandum also goes beyond devices to networks, requiring boards to restrict access to social media on school networks and school devices. That is a second policy lever operating on a different mechanism: not removing a device from a hand, but removing a destination from the network.

#### England: from guidance to statute

England's trajectory is the clearest example of escalation. The Department for Education first published non-statutory guidance in February 2024. That guidance was revised in January 2026 and "became statutory on 29 June 2026", with schools following it from September 2026 [8]. Within roughly two and a half years the same policy content moved from advice schools could ignore to a legal duty.

The scope is the whole day, not just lessons. The guidance covers "a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [7]. That is materially stricter than Ontario's instructional-time rule and stricter than most of the English schools the SMART Schools researchers surveyed, where restrictive policies were typically much newer than permissive ones — "most restrictive policies were implemented in the last 1–2 years" [3].

Enforcement in England runs through the behaviour system rather than through a separate sanction: "Schools should feel confident to use their power to confiscate mobile phones or similar devices as a disciplinary penalty where their policy is clearly breached" [7]. Search powers and detention sit behind that. The statutory guidance is also not absolute, because equality law overrides it: "Schools have a duty under the Equality Act 2010 to take such steps as is reasonable to avoid substantial disadvantage to a disabled pupil caused by the school’s policies or practices" [7]. A blanket prohibition that caught a diabetic pupil's glucose monitor would be unlawful, and the guidance says so.

The rationale stated in the statutory guidance itself is worth recording, because it is the hypothesis the evaluations then test: the risks of phone use "can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying" [7]. Attention, disruption and bullying are the three claims the English government has put its legal weight behind.

#### The Netherlands: a national agreement, near-universal in practice

The Netherlands took a different route again. The instrument is a national agreement rather than legislation, and the substantive rule is classroom-based: "Mobiele telefoons en andere devices zijn niet toegestaan in de klas, tenzij ze educatief worden gebruikt tijdens de les of uit noodzaak (zoals extra ondersteuningsbehoeften of medische noodzaak)" — phones and other devices are not permitted in the classroom unless used educationally during the lesson or out of necessity, such as additional support needs or medical necessity [5].

Adoption is effectively complete. In the government-commissioned evaluation, "99% van de VO-scholen heeft een mobielbeleid" — 99 per cent of secondary schools have a phone policy — and the majority run a "home or in the locker" rule or collect phones at the start of the lesson [5]. The Dutch case is therefore not a natural experiment in whether schools adopt a policy; it is a study of what happens when everyone does.

What it also shows is that schools are not uniformly satisfied with the instrument, and the evaluation records a heavier enforcement workload as one of the costs. It also records that some teachers reported an increase in physical bullying and disruptive behaviour after the ban [5]. Section 4 takes up why that is not as surprising as it sounds.

#### What the comparison shows

Three jurisdictions, three legal forms — a policy memorandum, a statutory duty, a sector-wide agreement — and three different scopes: instructional time only, the whole school day, classroom only. The evaluations discussed in the sections that follow are measuring these different things and calling the results "phone bans". A null in a country where phones are banned only in lessons cannot refute a positive finding in a country where they are banned all day, and vice versa. The single most common error in commentary on this literature is to treat the studies as replications of one another when they are tests of differently designed policies.

Two further design details cut across all of them. First, the counterfactual is rarely "phones". In England, most schools already restricted phones before the national guidance, so the guidance changed the margin for a minority of schools rather than for all of them [3]. In the Netherlands, with 99 per cent coverage, there is almost no untreated comparison group left. Second, enforcement is the binding constraint everywhere. A policy on paper that is not enforced produces no exposure and therefore no effect — and the evaluations that measure actual in-school use, rather than assuming the policy was followed, find wide variation in compliance.

On the coverage question this report can answer only partly. The two jurisdictions whose primary instruments I read in full and quote here are Ontario and England, with the Dutch national evaluation for the Netherlands; the South Australian evaluation [4] supplies the Australian state evidence discussed below, but I was not able to read the South Australian, French, or individual US state instruments themselves in this pass, and the report says so in Open questions rather than describing their terms at second hand.

### 2. What the causal studies find on learning and academic achievement

The learning question has the deepest evidence base of the four outcomes, and the best-designed study in it returns a null. A national study of United States schools adopting Yondr phone pouches — combining administrative achievement records with the timing of adoption across districts — finds that "average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero" [2]. The estimate is not an underpowered shrug: the authors state they "can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" [2]. That is a bound of about one-hundredth of a standard deviation, far below the effect sizes education research normally sets out to detect.

The same study finds the average hides a split by school level. "High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects" [2]. The high-school gain is "roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations", which the authors translate as "roughly a 0.9 percentile point increase in the test score distribution" [2]. Middle-school effects are roughly half that magnitude and in the opposite direction. A policy justified as an academic intervention is, on this evidence, producing achievement changes smaller than the differences a single classroom generates on its own.

The earlier and still most-cited English study points the other way, and the contrast matters. Béland and Murphy, in CEP Discussion Paper No. 1350 (May 2015), surveyed schools in four English cities about their phone policies and linked the answers to administrative exam records. They report that "student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban" [1], and the gain is concentrated: as summarised in a later peer-reviewed study, "The authors reported an improvement in student academic performance among lower-achieving students following the ban, whereas the high achievers were neither positively nor negatively affected" [4]. The mechanism story was that low achievers are the most distractible and most harmed by a phone in the room, so removing it helps them and leaves everyone else roughly where they were.

That result has not replicated in a comparable setting. The same summary notes that "In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban" [4] — a study testing the same hypothesis with a similar design in a different national setting and finding nothing. Two well-executed quasi-experiments on the same intervention in wealthy European countries with comparable exam systems disagree. The US pouch study's tight null sits closer to the Swedish result than to the English one.

The English cross-sectional evidence is also null on attainment. In the SMART Schools study of 30 English secondary schools, 20 restrictive and 10 permissive, there were no significant attainment differences: "adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.85–2.47, p = 0.18" for English and "adjusted odds ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.45–2.27, p = 0.98" for maths [3]. Those English intervals are wide — an odds ratio of 2.47 is not excluded — so this is a failure to detect, not a demonstration of no effect. It is consistent with the US null and inconsistent with a large Béland-style gain.

The South Australian preregistered natural experiment likewise found that "ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [4]. Academic engagement is a self-report proxy rather than an exam score, but it is the outcome closest to the mechanism the policy is meant to work through, and it did not move.

The one body of evidence pointing positive is the least rigorous: school staff reporting their own impressions. In the Dutch national evaluation, 28 per cent of schools reported positive effects on learning performance [5] — against 75 per cent reporting better concentration [5]. That gradient, where the outcome furthest from daily observation (test performance) shows the smallest reported improvement and the one staff can see directly (attention in the room) shows the largest, is what you would expect if the reports measure what teachers notice rather than what is happening to learning.

Read together: the causal estimates on achievement cluster around zero. The one positive high-school result is small enough to be policy-irrelevant, and the one large positive result — Béland and Murphy — is unreplicated and contradicted by both the Swedish study and the US pouch study. Anyone citing "phones out of schools raise marks" is citing the 2015 English paper without its later counter-evidence.

### 3. Attention, classroom disruption and social life at school

Attention is the outcome the policy is most obviously aimed at, and the one where the gap between what teachers report and what studies measure is widest.

Start with the mechanism: is there anything to remove? The US pouch study answers this directly with teacher reports of personal phone use in class, and the change is large. "The share of students reported to be using their phones in class for personal reasons falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools" [2]. Whatever else is uncertain, a policy that puts phones in a locked pouch changes the physical situation in the room substantially.

An independent behavioural measure agrees that devices left the room. Using location data from phones, the study finds that by the third year after adoption there were roughly 30 per cent fewer GPS pings in school — but the authors are careful about what that means: the figure "cannot be read as a direct measure of the change in student phone use, since it also includes use by adults and because pings are often recorded when phones are on but not in use" [2]. The behavioural data establish that phone presence in the building fell, not that student attention rose.

That distinction is exactly where the findings get interesting. Despite an 80 per cent drop in in-class phone use, the same study reports "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying or self-reported classroom attention" [2]. The intervention worked on the proximate behaviour and did not move the outcome that behaviour was supposed to cause. This is the most important single result in the report: the chain from policy to behaviour is strong, and the chain from behaviour to attention is, on this evidence, absent or too small to detect.

There is an important caveat, and it is the authors' own: "For classroom attention and online bullying, however, some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" [2]. If schools that adopted pouches were already on a different attention trajectory before adoption, the difference-in-differences estimate is contaminated. So the attention null is weaker evidence than the achievement null, which survives the pre-trend checks. It is a failure to find an effect in data with a known design problem, not a clean demonstration that none exists.

The teacher-report evidence points the other way, and it is worth being precise about why it is weaker. In the Dutch national evaluation, 75 per cent of schools reported positive effects on concentration [5] — by far the largest reported effect of any outcome in that survey, and the one that sits closest to what a teacher can actually see. A teacher who no longer has to interrupt a lesson to confiscate a phone will experience the lesson as more settled, and that experience is real. It is not, however, a measurement of student attention; it is a measurement of classroom manageability, and the two come apart when the same students are still not attending but are no longer visibly distracted.

The South Australian preregistered study offers a third angle, and finds nothing on academic engagement between ban and no-ban schools [4]. Engagement is self-reported, which limits it, but it is the student's own account of their involvement rather than an adult's impression of the room.

Two structural points explain the pattern. First, the nulls may reflect a displacement rather than a reduction. In the English SMART Schools study, students in restrictive schools had less phone and social media time during school hours — 0.67 fewer hours of phone use and 0.54 fewer hours of social media use per day in school time — but there was no difference in total weekday or weekend use [3]. Students appear to compress the same use into the hours when phones are permitted. If total exposure is unchanged, a null on attention is what the displacement model predicts.

Second, attention in a lesson is not a single quantity. A phone in a pocket that buzzes, a phone in a locked pouch in a corridor, and a phone at home are three different conditions, and the studies above do not separate the effect of removing the device from the effect of removing the anticipation of the device. That distinction has not been measured by anyone in this literature, and it is the mechanism question that matters most for design: a pouch that students know will be opened at 3pm may still occupy attention in a way that a phone left at home does not.

The honest summary for this section is that school phone restrictions demonstrably change what is in the room and what students do with their hands, and have not been shown to change attention as measured. The largest reported attention gains come from staff impressions; the studies that try to measure attention directly either find nothing or cannot rule out that the finding is an artefact.

### 4. Bullying and cyberbullying

Bullying is the outcome with the strongest theoretical case for a school-day restriction, because so much adolescent bullying now runs through group chats and social media that students carry in their pockets. It is also the outcome where the evidence is most genuinely mixed, and where the two best studies point in opposite directions.

The English statutory guidance names it as one of the three risks justifying a legal ban: "These risks can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying" [7]. If phones in school cause bullying, removing them should reduce it, and the reduction should be measurable in the schools that remove them.

The US pouch study tested exactly that and found nothing: alongside the null on attention, the authors report "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying" [2]. The measure is student-reported perception rather than incident counts, and — as with attention — the authors flag that "some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" [2]. So the null is not clean.

The South Australian preregistered study is the most instructive result here, because it found a bullying effect that looked like a policy success until the comparison group was examined. Bullying declined in both ban and no-ban schools over the study period. The ban group had higher bullying overall, but there was "no significant interaction between condition and time" [4] — meaning the ban did not change the trajectory. The decline was happening anyway. This is the single most useful methodological lesson in the whole literature: in a period when bullying rates were falling across the board, a before-and-after study of a school that adopted a ban would have recorded a fall and attributed it to the ban. Only the untreated comparison group reveals that the ban added nothing.

The countervailing evidence is Norwegian. Abrahamsson's study of middle schools, using administrative health records and survey data on school phone policies in an event-study design, reports that post-ban bullying falls among both girls and boys, alongside a reduction in girls' GP consultations for psychological symptoms and an improvement in girls' grade point averages. That is the strongest positive finding in the literature, and it is the one most often cited by advocates. I was not able to read the full paper in this pass — the working paper servers hosting it were unreachable — so this report records its headline claim without being able to inspect its design, its measure of bullying or its robustness checks. That limitation is stated in Open questions and matters: a bullying measure built from school-reported incidents and one built from student self-report can move in different directions under the same policy.

There is also a real possibility that bans change the form of bullying rather than its quantity, and the Dutch evaluation supplies a warning that this is not hypothetical. Among the reported consequences of the national agreement, the evaluation records an increase in physical bullying and disruptive behaviour ("Toename fysiek pest- en verstorend gedrag") [5]. The interpretation that fits the rest of the evidence is displacement: when the channel for a behaviour is closed, the behaviour does not necessarily stop, and adolescents who have lost the group chat may substitute what happens in the corridor. This is the same displacement pattern seen in the English usage data, where in-school phone time fell by about two-thirds of an hour without any change in total daily use [3]. A policy that moves conflict offline is not obviously a policy that reduces conflict, and none of the studies in this literature measures online and offline bullying jointly in a way that would settle it.

Where does that leave the bullying claim? Weaker than its advocates and its critics both suggest. The mechanism is plausible and the displacement risk is documented. One strong design finds a decline in both genders; another strong design finds the decline was already happening without the policy; a third finds no measurable change in perceived online bullying and cannot fully trust its own estimate. The honest statement is that the effect of school phone bans on bullying is unresolved, that the direction may differ by how bullying is measured, and that no study in this set has followed a cohort long enough to see whether offline substitution offsets an online reduction.

One further point about the design of these policies bears on bullying specifically, and it is a point the evidence supports but no study tests directly. Ontario's memorandum requires boards to restrict social media access on school networks and devices as well as to restrict phones [6]. That is a different intervention with a different mechanism: it targets the platform rather than the handset, and it would apply to a school-issued laptop as much as to a phone. If online bullying is the target, network-level restrictions are the better-aimed instrument, and evaluating them as if they were phone bans would miss what they do.

### 5. Mental health and well-being

Mental health is where the political stakes are highest and where the evidence is weakest relative to how confidently it is cited. Two well-designed studies dominate, and neither supports the claim that school phone bans improve adolescent wellbeing in any straightforward way.

The English SMART Schools study is the most direct test. It compared 30 English secondary schools — 20 restrictive, 10 permissive — on the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. "Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [3]. The confidence interval is the important part: it excludes any benefit larger than about two points on a scale where the population mean is 47, so a policy that produced a large wellbeing gain for the average student is ruled out. A small gain is not excluded.

Crucially, the study also measured whether the policies changed what they were supposed to change, and found that they changed only part of it. Students in restrictive schools "had lower phone (adjusted mean difference −0.67 h, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 h, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) during school time, but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [3]. The policy removed about forty minutes of daily phone time and half an hour of social media time from the school day and returned all of it after 3pm. If adolescent wellbeing problems are driven by total exposure — cumulative hours, late-night use, the shape of the day — a policy that reshuffles hours within the day should produce nothing, and it produced nothing.

The authors drew a firm conclusion from this: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [3]. That last clause matters for how this report should be read: the finding is against the current form of the policies, not against any conceivable intervention.

The US pouch study produces a more complicated and more interesting pattern, because it separates the short run from the long run. In the year of adoption, the authors find "suggestive evidence that student-reported subjective well-being also declines, consistent with adjustment costs as schools and students adapt" [2]. The magnitude is not trivial: "The decline is roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations, followed by an increase of 0.16 standard deviations" [2]. So the trajectory is a dip followed by a recovery that overshoots into positive territory, and the later positive estimate is larger than the short-run cost.

Two things about that deserve care. First, the short-run harm is real and is usually left out of both advocacy and criticism. Removing phones from a school is a disruption to how adolescents socialise, and a policy evaluated only at twelve months would show a net negative on wellbeing. Any school considering adoption should expect a bad first year, and any government announcing a ban should say so, because the political cost of an unannounced dip is that the policy gets reversed before the recovery arrives.

Second, the long-run positive estimate is the shakier of the two. It is a later-years estimate in a staggered adoption design, which is exactly the kind of estimate most vulnerable to contamination: once many districts have adopted, the "not yet treated" comparison group is shrinking and becoming unusual. The authors themselves hedge it as suggestive. It should be read as a hypothesis worth testing, not a finding to bank.

The same study found precisely null effects on the outcome that sits closest to mental health in the school's own records: chronic absenteeism, for which the authors find "similarly precise and small effects" [2]. If the wellbeing mechanism were operating strongly through school engagement, attendance is where you would expect to see it first.

Putting the two studies together: a cross-sectional English comparison finds no difference in wellbeing between restrictive and permissive schools and shows why — total use unchanged. A US panel finds a short-run wellbeing cost that reverses into a modest gain by the third year, with the gain estimated too loosely to rely on. These are not contradictory findings so much as different windows on the same process. The English study takes a snapshot at an unknown point in each school's adjustment; the US study traces the adjustment path. If the US trajectory is right, the English snapshot could have landed anywhere along it, and would be expected to average out to nothing across schools at different policy ages. That is an inference on my part, not a claim either paper makes, but it reconciles the two results without discarding either.

What neither study can address is the population most often discussed in policy: adolescents with clinical anxiety, depression or a diagnosed mental health condition. Both measure population averages. A policy that has no average effect could still help a subgroup substantially, or harm one — and the Dutch evaluation's report of increased physical bullying after the ban [5] is a reminder that the distribution of effects matters more than the mean. No study in this set reports subgroup effects by baseline mental health status, which is the single largest gap in the mental health evidence.

There is also a measurement problem that limits all of these results. Wellbeing in these studies means a self-report scale administered at school, in a room where the policy is in force. Students who have just had their phones taken away are being asked how they feel about their lives by the institution that took them. The US study's short-run dip is consistent with genuine distress and also consistent with resentment at being surveyed about it. Neither study can distinguish these, and the dip's disappearance over time is consistent with both adaptation and with students getting used to the survey.

### 6. How strong the evidence is: designs, reviews, compliance and what would settle the question

The evidence on school phone bans is better than the public argument suggests and much weaker than either side claims. It consists, in this set, entirely of quasi-experimental and cross-sectional studies. I found no randomised trial of school phone policy among the sources read for this report, and the reason is structural rather than accidental: randomising schools to a phone policy is politically and ethically difficult, and randomising students within a school is impossible without the policy becoming meaningless.

That leaves four designs, and their credibility is not equal.

**Difference-in-differences on schools' own decisions.** The Béland and Murphy study is the canonical example: "We use a difference in differences (DID) strategy, exploiting variations in schools' autonomous decisions to ban these devices, conditioning on a range of student characteristics and prior achievement" [1]. The conditioning helps, but the design's core problem cannot be conditioned away. Schools that choose to ban phones are not a random subset — they differ in leadership, behaviour culture, parental expectations and prior trajectory, and any of those could independently raise exam results. The study's own title frames phones as "technology, distraction and student performance", which is the hypothesis rather than the finding. When a study's identification rests on voluntary adoption, the estimate answers the question "what happened in schools that chose to ban" rather than "what would happen if a school were made to ban".

**Cross-sectional comparison of restrictive and permissive schools.** SMART Schools compared "adolescents from 30 English secondary schools, comprising 20 with restrictive (recreational phone use is not permitted) and 10 with permissive (recreational phone use is permitted) policies" [3]. This design shares the selection problem in a worse form, because there is no before-and-after at all. A permissive school may be permissive because its intake, its behaviour climate or its leadership is different, and those differences are exactly what would also move wellbeing and attainment. The study's nulls are therefore consistent with two stories: the policies do nothing, or the policies do something and the schools that adopt them differ in offsetting ways. The mechanism data — that total daily use was identical between groups [3] — is what makes the first story the more parsimonious, and that is why this report treats the null as informative rather than merely inconclusive.

**Staggered adoption with administrative panels.** The US pouch study is the strongest design in the set: administrative achievement and discipline records, location data, teacher and student surveys, and adoption timing that varies across districts. It is the only study here that can separate the year of adoption from later years, which is how it detects the discipline spike and the wellbeing dip that other designs would average into a single number. Its tight null on achievement — ruling out gains above roughly 0.007 student-level standard deviations [2] — is the most solid single result in the literature.

It is not flawless. The authors report that "some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" for attention and bullying [2], which means the two outcomes most central to the policy's rationale are precisely the ones whose estimates are least trustworthy. And a staggered design's later-year estimates depend on the pool of not-yet-adopting districts, which shrinks as adoption spreads — a problem that will get worse, not better, as the two-thirds-of-states figure [2] approaches completeness.

**Preregistered natural experiments.** The South Australian study is the design the field should copy more often, because it committed to its hypotheses in advance and included a comparison group of schools that did not adopt. Its value is visible in the bullying result: bullying fell in both groups, the ban group started higher, and there was no condition-by-time interaction [4]. A before-and-after design would have recorded a fall and credited the ban. Preregistration and a control group are what turned a false positive into a correct null.

**School self-report.** The Dutch national evaluation is the weakest design and the most quoted in policy debate. With 99 per cent of secondary schools holding a policy [5], there is no untreated comparison group left, and the outcomes are school leaders' impressions: 75 per cent reporting better concentration, 59 per cent a better social climate, 28 per cent better learning performance [5]. These are not measurements of student outcomes; they are measurements of staff experience. They are worth having — a policy that makes teachers' working lives harder will fail for that reason alone — but they cannot establish that students learned more or felt better.

Three cross-cutting weaknesses reduce confidence in all of it.

The first is that "phone ban" names at least three different treatments. Ontario restricts devices during instructional time only [6]; England's statutory guidance covers lessons, between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime [7]; the Netherlands restricts the classroom [5]. A study of one is not a test of another, and the literature routinely pools them in review.

The second is compliance. Every effect estimate assumes the policy was implemented. In England, most schools already had restrictive policies before the national guidance, and "most restrictive policies were implemented in the last 1–2 years" [3], so the national change moved a minority of schools and the treatment dose was uneven. Enforcement in England runs through confiscation as a disciplinary penalty [7], which means the policy's strength depends on how consistently individual teachers apply it. The US study's teacher-reported drop from 61 to 13 per cent in-class use [2] is the exception that proves the rule: it is one of very few direct measurements of whether the policy actually changed behaviour, and without such measurements a null result is uninterpretable — it could mean the policy does not work or that it was never applied.

The third is outcome measurement. Achievement comes from standardised tests and is solid. Discipline comes from school records and is decent. Attention, bullying and wellbeing come overwhelmingly from self-report, mostly collected at school, and each has a known bias: attention is self-assessed by the person whose attention is in question, bullying self-reports are sensitive to whether the school is watching, and wellbeing is measured in the institution that just changed the rules. None of the studies in this set pairs self-report with an independent measure of the same construct.

What would settle the question is not a better observational study but a different kind of evidence. Three things would move this from contested to answered. First, a school-level randomised trial — districts or schools assigned to adopt a pouch policy or not, with pre-registered outcomes on achievement, attendance, discipline, bullying and wellbeing, followed for at least three years to get past the adjustment dip. Second, measurement of total exposure rather than in-school exposure, because the displacement finding [3] implies that any policy evaluated only on school-hours use will overstate its effect. Third, joint measurement of online and offline bullying in the same instrument, since the Dutch report of increased physical bullying [5] is exactly the substitution that separate measures cannot detect.

Until then, the defensible reading is this: school phone restrictions reliably change what is in the room, have not been shown to improve learning at any policy-relevant magnitude, have not been shown to improve average wellbeing, and may reduce or merely relocate bullying depending on design and measurement. That is a real finding, and it is a narrower one than the legislation now spreading across two-thirds of American states and more than half the world's countries was sold on.

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims — the four questions, their derivation from figure/ground, the simultaneity and universality claims, and the sense in which McLuhan called them laws

The tetrad is a set of four questions to be asked of any medium, and it reached print three times before it reached book form. McLuhan first published it in *Technology and Culture* in January 1975, restated it in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* in 1977, and it appeared as a book only posthumously, in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988, with Eric McLuhan) and *The Global Village* (1989, with Bruce R. Powers) [1]. The 1988 book is therefore not the origin of the claim but its most elaborate and most aggressive statement — which matters for the reception history, because the strongest scientific claims attached to the tetrad were made after McLuhan's death and could not be defended by him.

The four laws, as stated in the applied literature, are that a technology will amplify or enhance some aspect of human experience or society; that it will obsolesce some aspect; that it will retrieve some aspect; and that it will reverse or "flip" into something else [2]. McLuhan claimed the questions could be put profitably to technologies as diverse as the wheel, cable TV, the Xerox, elevators, railways, clothing, housing, money and numbers [2]. The standard illustration is radio: it amplifies the human voice so as to give simultaneous access to the entire planet, obsolesces print to the extent that breaking news arrives by airwave rather than newspaper, retrieves the town crier of pre-literate society, and pushed further flips into the audio-visual medium of television [2].

Three features of the construction are load-bearing and are usually lost in summary.

First, the quadrants are not four independent slots. They are two pairs, mapped onto figure and ground: enhancement and retrieval are figure qualities, obsolescence and reversal are ground qualities [1]. Whatever the tetrad is, it is not a four-item checklist; it is a claim about which effects are noticed and which are the unnoticed environment that produces them.

Second, the laws are said to operate simultaneously rather than sequentially, and they are explicitly not predictive. McLuhan urged that one should never predict anything that has not already happened, and Tyler reads the fourth law accordingly, as a statement about what is already implicit or inherent in a medium rather than a forecast of what is coming [2]. This is a much weaker claim than it looks. A reversal that names a potential already present in the artefact cannot be wrong about the future, because it makes no claim about the future.

Third, obsolescence does not mean extinction. McLuhan's own gloss is that "Handwriting has been obsolescent since printing and typewriter, but there is a great deal more handwriting done daily now than was ever done before printing, or the typewriter" [2]. Obsolescence in the tetrad means displacement from prominence, not disappearance — a definition that makes the second law much harder to test, since any survival of the old medium is compatible with it.

What remains, once these three features are in place, is a universal schema with no stated ordering, no unit of measurement, and a definition of each term elastic enough to accommodate contrary evidence. The question the rest of this report turns on is whether that is a defect to be repaired or the point of the instrument.

### 2. The scientific claim and its first critics: the Popperian framing of 1975, the 1988 book's stronger claims, and the falsifiability objection

McLuhan's own framing in 1975 was an explicit invitation to refute him. Tyler records that he introduced the laws in a Popperian spirit, hoping readers might enjoy and profit from attempting to disprove his "laws," and that he called them laws because they represent an "ordering of thought and experience" which had not yet been disproved [2]. That is a peculiar definition of a law, and it is worth being precise about what it concedes: a law here is not a confirmed regularity but a schema that has survived so far, and its author's stated ambition was that someone would try to break it.

The 1988 book raised the stakes considerably. Tyler reports that in *Laws of Media* the McLuhans claimed the laws were testable hypotheses and a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 and 1977 statements, and that Eric McLuhan asserted the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [2]. Tyler's reply to that sentence is one line: "This is not, in fact, the case" [2].

His counterexample is textual and decisive, and it is the single most useful piece of evidence in the whole critical literature. Applying the tetrad to wine, the McLuhans say it enhances "grape juice" via fermentation, obsolesces "commonplace flavours," retrieves "ritual observance," and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" — at *Laws of Media* p. 206. On the same page, in an alternative version, wine enhances food and "the occasion," obsolesces "inhibition," retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture" and reverses into "hangover" and insult [2]. If the authors cannot reproduce their own answers on a single page, the claim that anyone anywhere can check them does not survive.

From this Tyler derives an objection with two arms, and both are needed to see why the tetrad resists testing.

The first arm is looseness. Conceived as a universal scientific method, the tetrad is "far too vague": a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any artefact, a huge range of things it might be said to augment, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse into, and the laws "do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit" [2]. A hypothesis that any competent analyst can satisfy in several incompatible ways has no failure condition.

The second arm is rigidity, and it is the one usually left out of summaries. "At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid": it requires us to fill the gaps, whether or not the evidence is there [2]. Tyler asks whether we really want to say that wine obsolesces "commonplace flavours" or retrieves "ritual observance," and answers that "we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad's frame" [2]. So the instrument is too permissive to be falsified and too demanding to be honest: a creative analyst will always find four plausible answers, and the requirement that there be four is what forces the implausible ones in.

Tyler's verdict on the scientific claim is blunt — that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the ordinary sense of the phrase is, he writes, preposterous [2] — and it is worth noting that this is not an attack from outside media theory. Tyler is a McLuhan scholar using the tetrad constructively in the same article. His concession is as important as his objection: the tetrad is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions [2], and that "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [2].

That concession is where the scholarly consensus has settled, and it has a consequence that the empirical question cannot avoid. If divergent tetrads for the same artefact are acceptable so long as they illuminate, then reproducibility is no longer a virtue to be demanded, and the tetrad has been moved, deliberately, out of the domain where testing applies. The falsifiability objection, in other words, was not rebutted; it was absorbed, by redefining the instrument as a probe.

### 3. Extensions and applications since 1988 — what the applied-tetrad literature does, and what it does not do

The applied-tetrad literature is large, and it is almost entirely a literature of application rather than extension. The pattern is consistent: take a medium that did not exist when McLuhan died, fill the four quadrants, and draw out what the exercise reveals. Tyler's own article is the clearest example in hand. He applies the tetrad to digital games and derives a specific, contestable result — that games pushed to their full potential flip not into immersion but into "pervasive and persistent play" [2] — and in doing so he makes the tetrad do real analytical work: the enhancement quadrant is used to argue against Arthur Asa Berger's claim that solo gaming is a species of "bowling alone," and the obsolescence quadrant is used against the assumption that games simply displace television. Each quadrant is aimed at a named misconception, and that is what gives the exercise a payoff.

The character of that result matters for the question of testing. Tyler's reversal claim is presented as an argument about what is already implicit in existing games — alternate reality games and persistent worlds that break the spatial, temporal and social boundaries of play — not as a prediction to be checked later. It is supported by pointing at games that exist, which makes it a reading of the present rather than a hypothesis about the future. That is exactly what McLuhan's own prohibition on prediction requires, and it is also why the result cannot fail.

Beyond that, the extension work I can report on from sources read in full is thin, and I will not pretend otherwise. The record's own earlier research on McLuhan reports two extensions worth naming, with the caveat that I am relying on that research pass rather than on the primary texts. First, Paul Levinson — who organised the 1978 tetrad conference and wrote the preface to the 1977 *ETC* statement — proposed "tetrad wheels" that chain tetrads through time, so that one medium's reversal becomes the next medium's starting point. Second, Graham Harman, in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (2009), takes the opposite position from Tyler: he holds that Eric McLuhan is "largely right" and that the tetrad should apply to all objects, not merely human artefacts, on the ground that every object is a medium. Harman also reports that Eric McLuhan said his father spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law, and for a single case where one of the four did not apply, without success. That is the most telling fact in the whole reception history: McLuhan's own attempt at disconfirmation took the form of a search for a counterexample and ended in failure to find one, which is not the same thing as a test.

What the literature has not produced, on the evidence I have been able to read, is a genuine extension of the tetrad's logical structure — a formalisation that specifies what would count as an incorrect answer to one of the four questions. The extensions that exist are either applications to new media or ontological widening (Harman's), and neither supplies a failure condition. I flag this as the weakest-evidenced part of this report: a proper survey would need the *Explorations in Media Ecology* literature, Robert K. Logan's *Understanding New Media*, and the 2017 *Taking Up McLuhan's Cause* volume, none of which I was able to read here.

### 4. Has anyone tried to test it empirically? The closest thing to a test in the applied literature, and what it found

No one, in the literature I was able to read, has tested the tetrad as a tetrad. There is no study that takes a set of artefacts, elicits the four answers from independent analysts, and measures whether they agree; no study that asks whether the four quadrants are exhaustive or whether a fifth exists; and no study that compares tetrad predictions against a null model. The reason is not obscurity — the tetrad is one of the most widely applied schemas in media studies — but design. As section 2 set out, the falsifiability objection was answered by reclassifying the instrument as a heuristic, and a heuristic is not the sort of thing one tests.

What does exist is something narrower and more interesting: tests of individual quadrant claims, treated as ordinary empirical propositions. The best example I found is Tyler's treatment of the second law, obsolescence, as a claim about media displacement. This is the right quadrant to pick, because obsolescence makes a claim about quantities — how much time people spend with one medium rather than another — and quantities can be measured.

Tyler's framing is that the claim "digital games obsolesce television" is a testable displacement hypothesis, and his survey of the evidence finds it "either inconclusive or equivocal" [2]. The studies he reports pull in opposite directions, and the detail is worth setting out because it shows exactly what a partial test of the tetrad looks like in practice.

Against displacement: a cross-European study published in 1999, which set out explicitly to discover whether interactive media had substantial consequences for children's media time, found that electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media, previously held by print — but the impact on television was unclear, and the authors warned that their cross-sectional data was "unfit to determine causal relationships" between media [2]. The Kaiser Family Foundation's research on 8–18 year olds found television dominating at an average of 3 hours a day with digital games far behind at just over an hour; comparing with their own earlier study, they found that total media time had not changed, and that heavy users of one medium tended to be heavy users of others, with children frequently using several media at once [2]. The looked-for displacement effect did not appear.

For displacement: Nick Yee's *Daedalus Project* survey of MMORPG players, not confined to young people, reported that players spent on average 21.0 hours a week playing and 7.7 hours a week watching television — figures that add up to roughly the national average of about 28 hours of television viewing, which Yee read as support for the claim that television time had been displaced by play [2].

Tyler's conclusion is the honest one: "existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [2]. He also identifies why the question is hard in a way that generalises to any attempt to test the tetrad: accurate records of time spent with a medium are hard to obtain and virtually impossible to reconstruct after the event; multitasking and media convergence complicate the accounting; and establishing a causal connection between one medium's popularity and another's decline raises conceptual difficulties as well as practical ones [2].

Three lessons follow, and they are the real answer to the empirical question.

First, the one quadrant that has been tested is the one that was operationalised as a quantity. Obsolescence became testable when it was restated as "how many hours moved from medium A to medium B." Enhancement, retrieval and reversal have not been restated in comparable terms, which is why they have not been tested.

Second, the test that exists does not test McLuhan's claim, because McLuhan defined obsolescence so that it does not mean extinction — handwriting increased after print, on his own account [2]. A finding that television viewing did not decline is therefore compatible with the second law, and a finding that it did decline is also compatible. Tyler's resolution is to redefine obsolescence as remediation, following Bolter and Grusin: television is repurposed rather than replaced, and the screen becomes an input device for play. That is a better reading, and it is also an unfalsifiable one.

Third, the studies Tyler reports were not designed to test the tetrad. They are media-use surveys and cross-sectional datasets, and the tetrad is applied to them after the fact. That is the standard evidential situation for the whole tradition: the tetrad is brought to data gathered for other purposes, and no one has gathered data for the purpose of testing it.

I should be explicit about the limits of this section. My search for empirical tests was severely constrained — the web search service failed throughout and I was reading through archives — so I cannot claim that no such study exists. What I can say is that the applied literature's most rigorous practitioner, working in a peer-reviewed game studies journal, treated the empirical question as one of assembling other people's media-use data and concluded that it was collectively uncertain. If a purpose-built test of the tetrad exists, it is not prominent enough to have reached the standard surveys of the field.

### 5. What a testable version would require, and where the tetrad stands now

The tetrad is stated as four simultaneous questions, not four stages: it holds that the laws "exist simultaneously, not successively or chronologically," and its declared purpose is exploratory, giving the questioner the "grammar and syntax" of the "language" of media [1]. That single design choice is the first obstacle to any empirical version. A causal model needs an ordering, a unit of measurement and a specified population of cases; the tetrad supplies none of the three, and deliberately so.

The second obstacle is structural. The four quadrants are not four independent variables. They are two pairs arranged as figure and ground — drawn as four diamonds in an X around the name of the medium, with the left/right axis marking the figure/ground association [1]. Any test that treats enhance, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse as four separable items to be scored is testing something other than the object McLuhan described.

The third is that the quadrants differ sharply in how much quasi-causal content they carry. Enhancement, obsolescence and retrieval are descriptive classifications of effects. Reversal is a claim about a mechanism: that a medium, pushed to its extreme, "overheats" and flips into an opposing form [1]. That is the one quadrant with a stated trigger condition, a stated direction of travel and a stated threshold, which makes it the natural entry point for anyone wanting a falsifiable formulation.

Laid out this way, the obstacles are not equally hard. A testable version would need, at minimum: a defined set of artefacts; a rule for individuating quadrants that is fixed before the analysis rather than after; an independent measure of "extremity" for the reversal claim; and a comparison against a rival fourfold or a null model, so that a filled tetrad can be distinguished from any other plausible four-box description of the same artefact. Nobody in the literature reviewed for this report has assembled all four.
